title: Viruses as Living Systems? Borrowed Closure and the Limits of Autopoiesis
content: In 2022, Yolles and Frieden argued that viruses are alive by moving the criterion for life from metabolism to organisation, arguing the genome–capsid couple to be autopoietic. This study reframes that conclusion with two constructs of Fisher-Generative Informational Realism (FGIR): the CAS/CAAS boundary, separating a Complex Adaptive System (CAS), adaptive but not self-sustaining, from a self-sustaining Complex Adaptive Autopoietic System (CAAS); and the coercivity law, which requires a system’s protoenergy, the informational effort of holding a configuration in persistent form, to exceed a threshold. The verdict “viruses are not autopoietic” conflates two conditions. Viruses satisfy the topological condition, the couple being a genuine self-producing network, but fail the resourcing condition, since the capacity to maintain it belongs to the host: “borrowed closure”, which we derive formally. Identifying the viral protoenergy with the draw on the host, and letting self-supply return only when the lineage’s translation machinery is complete, yields a host-budget equation with a saddle-node bifurcation at a critical completion fraction. Given a near-all-or-nothing return of self-supply, the barrier is structural rather than statistical, and it survives stochastic, epidemiological and delayed reformulations; its value is illustrative. The account is falsifiable and taxonomically agnostic, as the ribosome-encoding but host-dependent bacterium Carsonella ruddii shows, and crossings into self-sufficiency are observed only downward.
